questions.prompt: A friend says: 'Catholics worship statues.' A real, careful apologist should first ask:
choices: Is this real Catholic teaching or a caricature -- the Church distinguishes veneration from worship owed to God alone
How quickly can I win this argument outright, regardless of what the Church actually teaches
Whether the objection deserves any real response at all
Whether my friend is simply wrong about everything they believe
questions.correctAnswer: Is this real Catholic teaching or a caricature -- the Church distinguishes veneration from worship owed to God alone
questions.explanation: This is a real, common caricature -- the Church has always distinguished venerating an image (honoring what it represents) from the worship (latria) owed to God alone. Answering the real, actual teaching, not the caricature, is where a fruitful response has to start.
questions.hint: Consider whether this common claim actually matches what the Church herself teaches about images.

questions.prompt: Catholic apologetics responds to 'sola scriptura' (Scripture alone) by pointing out that:
choices: The New Testament itself never claims to be the sole rule of faith, and its own canon was discerned through Church Tradition
The Bible explicitly commands 'Scripture alone' in several clear passages
Tradition is a modern Catholic invention with no ancient roots
The earliest Christians had no oral teaching at all, only written texts
questions.correctAnswer: The New Testament itself never claims to be the sole rule of faith, and its own canon was discerned through Church Tradition
questions.explanation: Nowhere does the New Testament claim Scripture alone suffices -- and the very list of books making up the New Testament was itself settled through the Church's living Tradition, not by Scripture self-certifying its own contents.
questions.hint: Ask: who decided which books belong in the Bible in the first place?

citations.quote: Both Scripture and Tradition must be accepted and honored with equal sentiments of devotion and reverence.

questions.prompt: True or False: 2 Thessalonians 2:15 instructs believers to hold fast to traditions taught 'either by an oral statement or by a letter' from the apostles.
questions.explanation: This verse is a favorite apologetics proof-text: Paul explicitly places oral and written apostolic teaching on equal footing, undercutting the claim that only written Scripture carries authority.
questions.hint: Paul names two channels of teaching here, not just one.

citations.quote: Therefore, brothers, stand firm and hold fast to the traditions that you were taught, either by an oral statement or by a letter of ours.

questions.prompt: The Catechism teaches that Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition 'flow from the same divine wellspring' and together make up ____ sacred deposit of the Word of God.
questions.explanation: Scripture and Tradition are not two separate, competing sources -- together they form a single deposit of God's revealed word, entrusted to the Church.
questions.hint: It's a number -- the two together form only this many deposit.

citations.quote: a single sacred deposit of the Word of God

questions.prompt: The Bible's table of contents (its canon) was formally settled by:
choices: Church councils discerning, through apostolic Tradition, which books were truly inspired
A single apostle writing down a complete list before his death
A vote among ordinary lay believers across the empire
The Roman emperor Constantine at the Council of Nicaea
questions.correctAnswer: Church councils discerning, through apostolic Tradition, which books were truly inspired
questions.explanation: The canon wasn't simply self-evident -- the Church, exercising the authority Christ gave her, discerned which books were genuinely apostolic and inspired, a process later reaffirmed dogmatically at Trent.
questions.hint: Someone had to decide -- and it wasn't a Roman emperor or a popularity contest.

citations.quote: [The Synod] receives and venerates with an equal affection of piety and reverence all the books both of the Old and New Testament... as also the said traditions.
It was by the apostolic Tradition that the Church discerned which writings are to be included in the list of the sacred books.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Catholic Old Testament canon includes seven books, such as Tobit, Wisdom, and Sirach, that most Protestant Bibles exclude.
questions.explanation: These books, often called the deuterocanon, were part of the Greek Septuagint used by the early Church and were formally reaffirmed as canonical Scripture at the Council of Trent.
questions.hint: These books were part of the Greek Septuagint the early Church actually used, and Trent later confirmed them as Scripture.

citations.quote: [The Synod] receives and venerates with an equal affection of piety and reverence all the books both of the Old and New Testament... as also the said traditions.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning in the Scripture-and-Tradition relationship.

pairs.right: The inspired, written Word of God
God's Word handed down by the apostles, orally and in practice
The Church's living teaching office that authentically interprets both
The authoritative list of the Bible's inspired books

questions.explanation: None of these four stands alone -- Scripture and Tradition together form one deposit of revelation, and the Magisterium serves that deposit rather than standing above it.
questions.hint: One term names the written word, one the handed-down word, one the interpreting office, and one the official book list.

citations.quote: The task of giving an authentic interpretation of the Word of God, whether in its written form or in the form of Tradition, has been entrusted to the living teaching office of the Church alone.

questions.prompt: Sola scriptura holds that Scripture alone is the rule of faith. Applying that principle to itself, what problem appears?
choices: No book of Scripture teaches it, so by its own standard the doctrine cannot be established
It is taught only in the Old Testament, not the New
It is taught in Scripture but contradicted by Tradition
No problem appears; Scripture teaches it explicitly
questions.correctAnswer: No book of Scripture teaches it, so by its own standard the doctrine cannot be established
questions.explanation: This is the self-referential form of the dilemma. A rule stating that only Scripture may establish doctrine must itself be established from Scripture — and no text teaches it. It either fails its own test or admits an exception, and an exception is the thing it was formulated to exclude.
questions.hint: Apply the rule to the rule and see whether it survives.

questions.prompt: Paul tells the Thessalonians to hold fast to the traditions they were taught, 'either by an oral statement or by a letter of ours.' Why does this matter for the sola scriptura question?
choices: Scripture itself names oral teaching alongside written as binding, which is the position sola scriptura denies
It shows oral teaching replaced the written entirely
It applies only to Thessalonica and to no other church
It concerns liturgical custom rather than doctrine
questions.correctAnswer: Scripture itself names oral teaching alongside written as binding, which is the position sola scriptura denies
questions.explanation: The force here is that the text is doing the opposite of what the principle needs. Scripture does not merely fail to teach sola scriptura; in this passage it places oral and written transmission side by side as equally to be held.
questions.hint: Read what the verse puts on either side of 'either... or.'

questions.prompt: True or False: Saying Tradition is binding means the Church may add new revelation to what the apostles handed on.
questions.explanation: False, and the misunderstanding is common enough to be worth stating plainly. Public revelation closed with the apostles. Tradition is the handing on of that deposit and the growth in understanding it, not a channel through which new content arrives — which is precisely what the Church condemned in Montanism and again in Modernism.
questions.hint: Ask whether deepening the understanding of something and adding to it are the same act.

questions.prompt: Match each part of the sola scriptura dilemma to what it establishes.

pairs.right: No book lists the books; the list came from outside the text
The rule cannot be established by its own standard
Scripture itself binds oral teaching alongside written
A text read in contradictory ways needs more than the text to settle it

questions.explanation: Four independent pressures on one principle. They are worth keeping distinct: each stands alone, so answering one does not answer the others, and an argument that runs them together is easier to deflect than four that are made separately.
questions.hint: Each concerns a different thing: the list, the rule itself, a specific verse, and how disputes get settled.

questions.prompt: A friend asks: 'The Bible never mentions IVF or embryo research -- how can the Church have a real, confident position on something Scripture never addresses?' What is the real, positive answer this level offers?
choices: Scripture and Tradition hand on real principles the Magisterium can genuinely apply to a new question, without an explicit verse
Because the Church simply invents a new answer whenever a genuinely new question arises, with no real connection to anything already revealed
Because the Church actually has no real position on any question Scripture does not explicitly name
Because new moral questions are always left entirely to each individual believer's own private judgment
questions.correctAnswer: Scripture and Tradition hand on real principles the Magisterium can genuinely apply to a new question, without an explicit verse
questions.explanation: This is a real, positive answer to a real, common worry -- the Church does not need an explicit verse for every new question, because she already holds real, underlying principles from Scripture and Tradition that her living Magisterium can genuinely apply to whatever new, specific question actually arises.
questions.hint: Recall this topic's own earlier level on the Magisterium as the Church's own living teaching office, entrusted with authentic interpretation.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Catechism actually applies a real, existing principle -- the dignity of human life from its beginning -- directly to a modern question like embryo research.
questions.explanation: True, and this is exactly the real, positive process this level describes -- an underlying, already-revealed principle, genuinely applied by the Church's own living teaching authority to a specific, modern question Scripture itself never named.
questions.hint: Consider what this level's own real citation actually does with a real, underlying principle about human dignity.

questions.prompt: Why does this real, positive process -- principle plus living application -- actually answer the sola scriptura difficulty this topic's next level will name directly?
choices: A Bible-alone rule can't apply its own principles to new cases; the Church's living Magisterium can, generation after generation
Because sola scriptura and this process are, in fact, identical real approaches with no real difference between them
Because this process actually proves Scripture has no real authority in the Church's own decision-making at all
Because this process has no real connection to the difficulty a Bible-alone rule actually faces
questions.correctAnswer: A Bible-alone rule can't apply its own principles to new cases; the Church's living Magisterium can, generation after generation
questions.explanation: This is the real, positive contrast worth naming directly -- a text alone cannot apply itself to a case it never anticipated, but a real, living teaching authority, guided by the same Spirit who inspired the text, genuinely can, generation after generation.
questions.hint: Consider what a text alone can and cannot do, compared to a real, living teaching authority guided by the same Spirit.
